klo: Critically evaluate the coherence and credibility of the organisation’s strategic direction.
Appraise the assumptions, dependencies and uncertainties that influence the viability of strategic choices.
Judge the extent to which strategic priorities are differentiated, internally consistent and responsive to the operating environment.
Demonstrate executive confidence and collective accountability for the integrity of the chosen direction.

sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Use this tab to prepare before each section. It contains the unit intent, key facilitation questions, and tone and watch points for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Unit 4 tests whether the chosen direction is strategically sound. The four ABCV checkpoints (Arena, Boundaries, Competition and Value Proposition) and their Must-Be-True conditions turn assumptions into named, verifiable conditions with owners.
The ABCV–MBT Working Papers in Section 4 and the diagnosis exercise in Section 5 carry the unit. Insist on specific conditions and named owners.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
“What is your current strategy assuming about customers that nobody has verified?”
“Who else solves your customer’s problem, including those outside your industry?”
“Which ABCV checkpoint is your executive function least likely to examine? What risk does that create for the enterprise?”
“What is the one Must-Be-True condition your team is most likely to avoid naming, and who will verify it before the next strategic review?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points
Watch for: Must-Be-True conditions written as risks or concerns. Each must be a condition that is either true or false.
Watch for: competition defined as industry rivals only. Push for every alternative the customer can choose, including doing nothing.
Close: reserve the final minutes for the unnamed Must-Be-True question above. A named owner and date are the output.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.h2: What are the ABCV–MBT Integrity Checkpoints?
sections.sub: Interrogative Anchor · Leaders have defined their OKRs. Now the question is whether they are strategically sound. The ABCV–MBT framework is the stress test for reality.
slo: Recognise why well-formulated objectives can still lack strategic credibility.
Distinguish objectives that are measurable from those that are strategically coherent.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1 · Awareness

Section intent: This opening section introduces the ABCV–MBT framework as a strategic integrity filter. Create a felt sense of productive discomfort: "Are our OKRs actually grounded in reality?" Leaders must feel the danger of unnamed assumptions before they can value the discipline of naming them.

Opening frame: Before content, ask: "How many of you have experienced a well-crafted strategy that fell apart once execution started because of assumptions we hadn't named until they broke?" Pause. Use the silence. Then introduce ABCV–MBT as the tool that names those invisible assumptions before they become expensive failures.

On the checkpoint cards: Invite leaders to expand each card and pause on the MBT condition. Ask them to mentally apply it to one of their own Key Results before the group moves on. Suggested section time: 20–25 minutes.

parts.title: 1.1 — The Problem with Well-Written OKRs
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1
Key message: Most strategies fail from unnamed conditions. The cost of discovering those conditions during execution is exponentially higher than naming them now.

Discussion prompt: "Think of a goal that failed in your organisation. Was it a lack of effort, or was there an assumption that turned out to be wrong — one you didn't name until it broke?" Suggested time: 5–7 minutes.
content: The leaders have done the hard work of defining what 'Success in Practice' looks like. They have translated those visions into OKRs that look great on paper — measurable, ambitious, and with deadlines.
The next step is to move past 'well-written' OKRs and ask: are they strategically sound?

Most strategies fail because of 'unnamed conditions.' We often build our goals on a bed of invisible assumptions that we only discover once execution begins and things start to break. By then, the cost of correction is massive.

The ABCV–MBT framework is the 'stress test' for reality. ABCV gives the interrogation structure — the four checkpoints of strategy. MBT (Must-Be-True) forces leaders to name the 'load-bearing walls' of their goals. For every checkpoint, leaders must identify the specific condition that must remain true for their Key Result to survive. This ensures OKRs are anchored in the real world.
The ABCV–MBT Checkpoints serve as a strategic early-warning system. By surfacing conditions now, we plan for success and build the resilience to handle the moment the world changes.

parts.title: 1.2 — The Four ABCV Integrity Checkpoints
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2

Directing participants: Ask leaders to expand each checkpoint card and pause on the Must-Be-True condition. Invite them to mentally test one of their team's Key Results against each MBT before group discussion. Do not allow the group to rush through all four in rapid succession — each deserves a moment of real reflection.
The ARENA card typically surfaces enough recognition to anchor the whole framework — use it as the gateway. Suggested time: 10–12 minutes including reflection.
Facilitator Move — After the Cards

Ask: "If you had to identify the single ABCV checkpoint your organisation most consistently overlooks when setting strategy — which would it be? And what has that cost you?" The answers surface role-based blind spots you will revisit in the Extrapolating section.
content: Expand each checkpoint below to explore the strategic logic, the interrogation question, and the Must-Be-True condition that anchors it.
Arena
Customer End Game
Strategic Logic
Strategy starts with a shift in perspective: we compete for a customer need. If we define our arena by our products, we miss the forest for the trees.
Interrogative Anchor
What is the customer actually trying to achieve? What functional, emotional, or social 'job' are they hiring us to do?
Must-Be-True Condition
What must remain true about customer behaviour or demand for this Key Result to stay relevant?
Boundaries
Friction Architecture
Strategic Logic
Every arena has invisible walls: operational limits, regulations, or simple human resistance to change. A strategy that ignores friction is a wish.
Interrogative Anchor
What is going to push back against us? What internal or external friction could slow this Key Result down or stop it entirely?
Must-Be-True Condition
What must remain true operationally or regulatorily for us to actually deliver this without breaking?
Competition
The True Landscape
Strategic Logic
Once you define the Arena by the customer's need, your 'competitors' change. You are fighting anyone who solves that same problem in a different way, peers included.
Interrogative Anchor
Who else is solving this problem — even if they look nothing like us? Who is the 'alternative' the customer might choose?
Must-Be-True Condition
What must remain true about our specific advantage compared to these other options?
Value Proposition
Coherent Advantage
Strategic Logic
Strategy wins when you are distinct. Every Key Result should make your unique DNA stronger. If a goal dilutes your brand or confuses your value, it's a distraction.
Interrogative Anchor
How does this goal make us more 'us'? Does this Key Result sharpen our distinctive edge or just add noise?
Must-Be-True Condition
What must remain true about our value architecture for this Key Result to stay coherent and profitable?

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.sub: Ignition Point · Most strategic plans look bulletproof on paper. They wither in execution under the weight of unexamined assumptions left unnamed.
slo: Judge whether strategic priorities respond to the outcomes customers pursue.
Articulate the assumptions on which each strategic objective depends.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2 · Intelligence

Section intent: Shift leaders from passive understanding to personal conviction. They should finish this section believing their current planning process has a structural blind spot that this framework corrects. The goal is recognition.

Opening provocation: "We instinctively define ourselves by our business cards. But here is the cold truth: industry categories were made for administrators." Pause. Let it land. Then ask who has been stung by a competitor they didn't see coming. Suggested section time: 20–25 minutes.

parts.title: 2.1 — The Industry Illusion & the Arena Shift
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.1

The Nokia moment: Use the smartphone analogy specifically. Nokia defined themselves as a telecoms company. The smartphone redefined the arena entirely. Ask: "Who in your industry is playing a different game that you're only just starting to notice?"

The three dimensions: After presenting Functional, Emotional, Social needs, ask leaders to apply them to their primary customer. Most find the Emotional and Social dimensions are rarely discussed in their strategy sessions — which is exactly the blind spot. Suggested time: 6–8 minutes.
Facilitator Example — Netflix

Functionally: video. Emotionally: escape. Socially: connection to the global water-cooler conversation. If Netflix had only thought they were in the “DVD-by-mail industry,” they'd be a footnote in history. Ask: "What industry definition is keeping your organisation from seeing its true arena?"
content: The cold truth: Industry categories were made for administrators. Customers wake up thinking: “I need to feel secure about my family's future.” When we define our world by our industry, we watch our traditional neighbours while a stranger from a different 'industry' walks away with our customers.
The Three Dimensions of Customer Need
Functional
The actual task they need to finish. The concrete outcome they are paying for.
Emotional
How they want to feel while doing it. “I want to feel in control.” “I want this to be effortless.”
Social
How they want others to see them. “I want to be seen as a pioneer.” “I want credibility.”

parts.title: 2.2 — Naming the Must-Be-Trues
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.2

The MBT concept: Help leaders distinguish between a strategy and a hope. Use this language: "Every OKR is built on assumptions. MBT forces you to name them out loud — because if you can't name them, you can't monitor them, and if you can't monitor them, you can't protect your strategy."
Practical check: Ask each leader to try naming one MBT condition for one of their Key Results right now. If they struggle, that difficulty is itself the lesson. Suggested time: 7–8 minutes.
content: Even a strong checkpoint can miss a hidden crack. Every strategy is built on a “load-bearing” assumption — something we believe to be true but haven't said out loud. The MBT turns these whispers into explicit commitments.
ARENAAre we solving a real customer end-game, or just pushing a product?
BOUNDARIESWhat are the “laws of physics” here? What regulations or internal frictions will push back?
COMPETITIONWho else is solving this problem — even the competitors who don't look like us?
VALUE PROPDoes this goal actually make us more distinct, or are we just blending in?

By naming MBT conditions, we transform strategy from a “hopeful ambition” into a tested commitment. The ABCV–MBT checkpoints ensure that when you hit the gas, the wheels are actually attached to the car.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Does Directional Integrity Break Down?
sections.sub: The Alignment Brigade · Every executive role is trained to protect a different part of the enterprise system. These specialisations create selective attention — and predictable strategic blind spots across the leadership mandate.
slo: Identify the dimensions of strategic integrity most often overlooked in their own executive function.
Appraise how functional blind spots compound into enterprise-wide strategic risk.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3 · Extrapolating

Section intent: Make the ABCV framework personal to each leader's role. The aim is illumination. Leaders should finish knowing which ABCV checkpoint is most likely their organisational blind spot and why it creates specific downstream consequences.

On the hot zone grid: Ask each leader to click their own role card first. Then invite the group: "Look at the gaps across all roles. Which checkpoint appears most frequently as an overlooked dimension?" That answer is the team's most critical strategic vulnerability. Suggested section time: 20–25 minutes.

parts.title: 3.1 — The Executive Hot Zone: Role-Based Blind Spots
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3.1

The key insight: The “What they start asking” column shows the symptoms — the questions leaders only ask when the underlying ABCV condition has already failed. These are late signals. ABCV–MBT creates early signals.

Facilitation move: After the group has explored the grid: "Which of these symptoms have you heard in your leadership conversations in the last quarter? What does that tell you about where your blind spot sits?" Suggested time: 10–12 minutes.
content: Click a role below to see what typically gets overlooked, what it feels like in the organisation, and what questions leaders begin asking when the condition has already failed.
CEO
Chief Executive
CFO
Chief Financial
COO
Chief Operating
CHRO
Chief Human Resources
CTO
Chief Technology
CMO
Chief Marketing
CCO
Chief Commercial
CPO
Chief Procurement
CSO

What Gets Overlooked
Boundaries. The CEO holds the vision and drives narrative — but operational friction is rarely in the chief executive's focus until execution stalls significantly.
⚠ Symptom: “Why are we not seeing the results when our strategy is clear?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Boundaries checkpoint forces explicit naming of the regulatory, structural, and behavioural friction standing between the vision and its delivery. Vision without friction-mapping is only a speech.
✓ Right question: “What specific conditions must remain true for execution to sustain the pace we've planned for?”
What Gets Overlooked
Arena. The CFO tracks whether the model works — but whether the underlying customer demand is still real and growing is often outside the financial reporting frame.
⚠ Symptom: “The model works… so why is performance lagging?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Arena checkpoint reframes financial health as dependent on customer-need relevance. Revenue can be temporarily maintained even as the underlying arena is shifting away from your value proposition.
✓ Right question: “Is the customer end-game we designed this model around still the right end-game?”
What Gets Overlooked
Competition. Operational leaders optimise the machine — but if the machine is serving the wrong arena, efficiency just accelerates the organisation in the wrong direction.
⚠ Symptom: “We've optimised everything — what are we missing?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Competition checkpoint asks: who else is solving the customer's problem, even those who look nothing like us? Operational excellence means nothing if the alternatives are more convenient for the customer.
✓ Right question: “Are our efficiency gains making us meaningfully more competitive against the real alternatives customers have?”
What Gets Overlooked
Competition. People alignment and engagement are the CHRO's primary checkpoint — but a highly engaged team executing the wrong strategy still loses to a competitor solving the problem better.
⚠ Symptom: “Our people are committed — why isn't it translating?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Competition checkpoint reveals that motivation and alignment are necessary but insufficient if strategic direction points at the wrong competitive target. Energy without direction is enthusiasm without results.
✓ Right question: “Are we aligning our people's energy toward the right competitive arena, or building capability for yesterday's contest?”
What Gets Overlooked
Arena. Technical delivery is the CTO's primary accountability — but whether the solution addresses the customer's actual end-game (functional, emotional, social) is often assumed and left untested.
⚠ Symptom: “We delivered the system — why isn't adoption there?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Arena checkpoint asks: did we build for what the customer is actually trying to achieve — or for the specification handed to us? These are not always the same thing. Adoption requires arena-alignment as well as technical delivery.
✓ Right question: “Does this solution address the functional, emotional, and social outcome the customer is actually pursuing?”
What Gets Overlooked
Boundaries. The CMO creates demand — but if the operational infrastructure cannot fulfil that demand, the campaign creates frustration and brand damage.
⚠ Symptom: “We created demand — why can't we fulfil it?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals
The Boundaries checkpoint identifies the internal and external friction that must remain within tolerance for demand to convert to delivered value. Demand without delivery capacity is brand erosion.
✓ Right question: “Do our operational boundaries allow us to fulfil the demand our marketing is designed to generate?”
What Gets Overlooked

Value Proposition. Revenue growth is the CCO's scorecard — but growing by winning the wrong business can dilute the organisation's distinctive identity and long-term positioning in ways that compound over time.
⚠ Symptom: “We're closing deals — but at what cost to who we are?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals
The Value Proposition checkpoint asks: does this contract strengthen or dilute our distinctive edge? Not all revenue is strategic revenue. Some growth makes the organisation less coherent.
✓ Right question: “Does this deal sharpen our value architecture or compromise it for short-term volume?”
What Gets Overlooked
Arena. Cost reduction and supply chain resilience are the CPO's primary mandate — but savings that are not connected to the customer's end-game do not translate into strategic progress.
⚠ Symptom: “We've saved money — but has it actually mattered?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Arena checkpoint asks: does this procurement decision improve our ability to deliver on the customer's actual need? Cost efficiency that doesn't serve the customer's end-game is operational tidiness.
✓ Right question: “Does this cost initiative strengthen our ability to compete in the arena our customers actually operate in?”
What Gets Overlooked
Boundaries. Strategy clarity is the CSO's domain — but without explicit identification of operational friction, strategies that are coherent in design break down repeatedly in execution.
⚠ Symptom: “Why does execution keep breaking after alignment?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Boundaries checkpoint identifies structural, cultural, and regulatory friction points that strategy must be designed around. Clarity without friction-mapping is strategy without implementation physics.
✓ Right question: “Which operational friction points have we built our strategy around — and which are we still hoping won't materialise?”

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: From individual insight to collective strategic commitment
slo: Appraise the assumptions, dependencies and uncertainties behind the organisation’s strategic objectives.
Demonstrate collective accountability by assigning ownership for verifying critical conditions.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4 · Integration

Section intent: This is where individual strategic reasoning becomes a shared leadership artefact. The four steps move the group from personal analysis (Step 1) through collective synthesis (Step 2) to ownership assignment (Step 3) and partner mapping (Step 4). Each step builds on the previous — do not skip.

Pacing: Step 1 is individual and takes 15–20 minutes. Steps 2–4 are collective and take 20–30 minutes together. Build in transition time between individual and group phases. Suggested total section time: 40–50 minutes.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Step 1

Briefing for participants: Each person works independently. They select up to three objectives from their current OKR/strategic plan and apply all four ABCV checkpoints to each. The MBT condition they name must be specific enough that someone else could attempt to verify it. Vague MBTs (“the market must support us”) are not sufficient — push for precision.

Watch for: Participants who struggle to name MBT conditions. This is a signal that the objective itself may not be sufficiently grounded. Use this as productive friction: “If you cannot name a Must-Be-True, what does that tell you about this objective?”
◆ PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete the ABCV–MBT analysis in Step 1 of their own file: up to three current strategic objectives, with one Must-Be-True condition per checkpoint.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Step 2

Process: Ask each participant to share one MBT condition from each checkpoint they found most revealing. Look for patterns: which checkpoint recurs as most challenging? Which MBT conditions appear in multiple participants’ papers? These are your organisation’s strategic pressure points.

Key facilitation move: Where participants disagree on what the MBT condition should be, do not resolve the disagreement prematurely. Disagreement on MBTs often signals that the objective itself has not been defined precisely enough. Sit in that discomfort productively. Suggested time: 15–20 minutes.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Participants capture the shared themes, strategic disagreements and top five priority MBT conditions in their own worksheet. Ask one participant to read the agreed top five aloud, then test each with: ‘What evidence would prove this condition is true?’
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Step 3

Key distinction: “Lead Owner” means the person accountable for ensuring the MBT condition is verified before the dependent strategy is executed. Every MBT must have a named owner — shared ownership is no ownership.

Watch for: Leaders who assign themselves as owner of every high-priority MBT — this signals either genuine accountability or reluctance to trust colleagues. Leaders who avoid ownership of any MBT — this signals disengagement from the strategic process. Both are worth naming. Suggested time: 10–15 minutes.
◆ PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants assign a lead owner to each priority MBT condition from Step 2 in Step 3 of their own file.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Step 4

Purpose: MBT verification rarely falls within the ownership of a single leader. This step surfaces the cross-functional coordination required to confirm or disconfirm each condition. It often reveals that the organisation’s structures make verification harder than it should be — which is itself a strategic insight.

Closing the integration: End this section with a commitment question: “Which one MBT condition, if left unverified, represents the greatest risk to our strategy’s integrity? Who is leaving this room responsible for that verification?” Suggested time: 10–15 minutes.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Participants record the evidence, data sources and verification timeline in their worksheet. Before closing, confirm every priority MBT condition has a named owner and a date.
content: Team Exercise · Collective Intelligence

This is a group exercise. Working from the shared case study below, each leader first analyses the strategy individually in their executive role (Step 1). You then consolidate those perspectives as a leadership team across Steps 2–4 — turning individual judgement into a single collective view of the strategy’s integrity.
Shared Case Study

Meridian Health Group. A regional private-hospital group built its reputation on premium, in-person specialist care. Under margin pressure and the rapid rise of tele-health, the board has approved a strategy to launch a digital-first virtual-care platform aimed at younger, lower-acuity patients — while sustaining the premium specialist business that defines the brand. Leadership is confident in the financial model and the technology. As the executive team, your task is to stress-test this strategic direction through the four ABCV checkpoints before execution begins, and to name the Must-Be-True conditions the strategy is silently assuming.
Step 1Individual Working Paper
Step 2Consensus & Synthesis
Step 3Leadership Ownership
Step 4Supporting Partners

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.h2: Cause of Death — Match the Breakdown
sections.sub: Diagnose the strategic failure. Defuse the mine before it detonates.
slo: Evaluate realistic strategic failures to diagnose where directional integrity broke down.
Judge which integrity checkpoint would have protected the chosen direction.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5 · Application

Section intent: Learners apply ABCV diagnostic thinking under pressure. Each scenario is a real-world strategy failure. The mine mechanic rewards precision — guessing the right checkpoint for the wrong reason will eventually surface. Push participants to articulate their reasoning before selecting an answer.
Debrief move: After the game, ask: “Which mine was hardest to defuse? What does that tell you about your organisation’s own ABCV blind spot?” Suggested section time: 20–25 minutes.
📌 Facilitator: The Answer Key accordion below is visible only in this facilitator file. Participants see the same game without the key.
content: Score
pts | max 8
0 / 4 mines defused
💣 Mine 1 — The Ghost Ship

A SaaS platform achieved 85% retention in year one. By year three, churn reached 70%. Nothing in the product changed. Support tickets were low. The platform worked exactly as designed. Post-exit interviews revealed: customers had changed what they were trying to achieve — and the platform never followed.
SELECT THE INVESTIGATION QUESTION
SELECT THE ABCV CHECKPOINT
💣 Mine 2 — The Ferrari in the Mud

A leading logistics firm invested R120m in a new digital operations platform. Eighteen months in, less than 30% of staff were using it consistently. Field teams had developed workarounds. Middle management had quietly reverted to spreadsheets. The system was technically excellent. The organisation was not designed to absorb it.
SELECT THE INVESTIGATION QUESTION
SELECT THE ABCV CHECKPOINT
💣 Mine 3 — The Invisible Disruption

A financial advisory firm was ranked #1 in client satisfaction for four consecutive years. Then revenue began declining. No competitor had taken their clients. No scandal. No service failure. The problem: a fintech app was letting clients self-manage what the firm had always managed for them — and clients preferred it for 60% of use cases.
SELECT THE INVESTIGATION QUESTION
SELECT THE ABCV CHECKPOINT
💣 Mine 4 — The Identity Crisis

A boutique consulting firm built its reputation on deep-sector expertise and bespoke strategy work. Under revenue pressure, they began accepting large implementation contracts — work that paid well but required different skills, different team profiles, and a different culture. Within two years, they won more work but lost their most experienced strategists and their distinctiveness with clients who valued exactly what they had been.
SELECT THE INVESTIGATION QUESTION
SELECT THE ABCV CHECKPOINT

parts.title: Unit Summary
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Unit Summary

Closing the unit: Unit 4 reframes strategy integrity as a testable condition. Use the final five minutes to ask: “What is the one MBT condition your team is most likely to avoid naming? Why? And what will you do about it before the next strategic review?”
content: This session was about ensuring strategic direction is structurally sound before the first move of execution is made. We’ve all seen well-written OKRs collapse because the assumptions holding them up were never tested. The ABCV–MBT framework served as our strategic integrity filter: the stress test to ensure Key Results are anchored in customer reality, resilient to friction, and true to the organisation’s identity.
Here is a recap of how we moved from individual functional perspectives to a unified executive judgement.
1 — Awareness: The Integrity Checkpoints
We began with the What. The ABCV checkpoints interrogated strategy across four critical dimensions:
Arena — The specific customer end-game we are playing for.
Boundaries — The operational or regulatory “clog points” that could slow us down.
Competition — All the alternatives, including direct rivals, competing for the same need.
Value Proposition — The distinctive edge that defines our organisational identity.

For every checkpoint, the team identified the Must-Be-True (MBT) condition — the “load-bearing” assumption that must hold for the strategy to survive. This is the early warning system: exposing risks before they become expensive failures.
2 — Intelligence: Why Strategic Integrity Matters
This stage explored the Why. Most strategies fail because of unexamined assumptions.

We shifted thinking from rigid industry categories to Customer Arenas, recognising that customers chase functional, emotional, and social outcomes. By naming MBT conditions early, the team moved the strategy from a hopeful ambition to a battle-tested commitment.
3 — Extrapolating: Locating the Blind Spots
Next, the Where. Every CXO sees the world through a specialised perspective:
CEOs lean toward narrative and stakeholder credibility
CFOs hunt for financial viability and return logic
COOs focus on operational feasibility and delivery rhythm
CHROs look at culture and leadership readiness

While these perspectives are vital, they naturally create selective attention. Applying the ABCV–MBT checkpoints across all roles surfaced the hidden risks that usually only emerge halfway through the execution cycle.
4 — Integration: Collective Intelligence

The session culminated in the Converging Zone — the moment the team consolidated individual perspectives into a single enterprise interpretation. By reviewing consolidated responses, the team was able to:
Identify patterns of agreement and surface strategic disagreements
Determine the most critical “deal-breaker” execution conditions
Agree on the severity of the MBT requirements
The ABCV–MBT checkpoints have transformed your OKRs from polished aspirations into resilient execution signals, grounded in the hard realities of the enterprise system.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Understanding why well-written objectives still fail — and the four conditions that determine whether they hold
slo: Recognise why well-formulated objectives can still lack strategic credibility.
Distinguish objectives that are measurable from those that are strategically coherent.

parts.title: 1.1 — The Problem with Well-Written OKRs
content: A well-written OKR can still fail when the strategic conditions it assumed — the Arena, the Boundaries, the Competition, the Value Proposition — were never verified before execution began.

This is the problem ABCV-MBT solves. It moves strategy from belief to testable commitment by naming the conditions that must be true for a strategy to hold — and then requiring leaders to verify them.
The Must-Be-True (MBT) Condition

A Must-Be-True condition is a specific, verifiable assumption that a strategic objective requires in order to remain valid. It is a named condition: either it is true, or the objective rests on unstable ground.
The power of naming MBTs lies in what naming reveals: which parts of the strategy have been confirmed, and which parts have simply been assumed.
✎ Reflection
Think of a current strategic objective your organisation is pursuing. What is it assuming about the world that has not yet been verified?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Think of a current strategic objective your organisation is pursuing. What is it assuming about the world that has not yet been verified?

parts.title: 1.2 — The Four ABCV Integrity Checkpoints
content: ABCV provides four checkpoints through which to test the integrity of any strategic direction. Click each checkpoint to explore what it examines, the question it asks, and the Must-Be-True condition it requires.
Arena
Customer End Game

Strategic Logic: A strategy is only as valid as the customer outcome it is designed to deliver. Arena defines the precise destination: the functional, emotional, and social outcome the customer is truly pursuing.
When Arena is not verified, strategy can be perfectly executed in the wrong direction. The product works. The team performs. But the customer has moved on to a different end-game.
➤ Interrogative Anchor: What functional, emotional, and social outcome is the customer truly pursuing — and has it shifted?
MBT Condition: The customer outcome we have designed this strategy around is still the right outcome — and has not materially shifted since our last verified check.
Boundaries
Friction Architecture

Strategic Logic: Every strategy operates within a friction architecture — the regulatory, structural, and behavioural constraints that determine what can and cannot be delivered. Boundaries names these explicitly so that strategy is designed around real constraints.
A strategy that ignores its Boundaries produces plans that are coherent in design and impossible in execution. The friction was always there; it simply wasn’t named.
➤ Interrogative Anchor: What internal or external friction is preventing strategy from delivering at scale?
MBT Condition: The regulatory, structural, and behavioural constraints operating on this strategy remain within a range that our execution model can absorb.
Competition
True Landscape

Strategic Logic: Competition is not limited to those who look like you. The true competitive landscape includes all alternatives the customer can choose — including doing nothing, self-service, or a solution from an entirely different industry.
Organisations that define competition too narrowly build advantage against the wrong rivals. Disruption almost always arrives from outside the frame they were watching.
➤ Interrogative Anchor: Who else is solving this problem — including those who don’t look like competitors?
MBT Condition: The competitive landscape we have mapped includes all meaningful alternatives the customer has, including traditional industry rivals.
Value Proposition
Coherent Advantage

Strategic Logic: A value proposition is the coherent set of choices — what you do, what you do not do, and why your combination of both is difficult to replicate — that creates defensible advantage in the Arena you have chosen.
Strategies that expand too broadly, or accept the wrong kind of growth, erode the Value Proposition over time. Distinctiveness must be maintained by design, checked at each strategic decision.
➤ Interrogative Anchor: Does our distinctive value architecture still create coherent, defensible advantage?
MBT Condition: The strategic choices we are making with this objective strengthen — or at minimum do not dilute — our distinctive value architecture.
✎ Reflection
Which of the four ABCV checkpoints is your organisation least likely to examine rigorously before launching a new strategic initiative? What does that pattern cost you?

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.sub: The strategic failures that ABCV is designed to prevent — and why naming conditions changes what leaders are responsible for
slo: Judge whether strategic priorities respond to the outcomes customers pursue.
Articulate the assumptions on which each strategic objective depends.

parts.title: 2.1 — The Industry Illusion & the Arena Shift
content: Nokia built the best phones in the world for the market that existed. But the Arena had shifted: the customer’s end-game had become a connected, intelligent, personalised device. Nokia’s execution was excellent. Its Arena was wrong.

Netflix understood something Blockbuster did not: the customer’s true end-game was frictionless access to content. The Arena had always been about convenience and selection. Blockbuster optimised the store. Netflix redefined what the store was for.
The Arena has three dimensions that must all be examined:
Functional — What specific task or problem the customer needs resolved
Emotional — How the customer wants to feel during and after the experience
Social — How the customer wants to be seen by others through their choice

Most strategies address the functional dimension adequately. The emotional and social dimensions are where strategic drift goes undetected — and where early Arena shifts first become visible, if leaders are asking the right questions.
✎ Reflection
In your own market, which of the three Arena dimensions (functional, emotional, social) is changing fastest? What does that tell you about the MBT conditions your strategy currently assumes?
prompts: ✎ Reflection In your own market, which of the three Arena dimensions (functional, emotional, social) is changing fastest? What does that tell you about the MBT conditions your strategy currently assumes?

parts.title: 2.2 — Naming the Must-Be-Trues
content: An MBT condition is a specific, named condition that can be investigated, confirmed, or disconfirmed. The act of naming it is an act of strategic honesty: this is what we are betting on.
Each ABCV checkpoint generates a different category of MBT condition:
Arena MBTs — Conditions about what the customer is truly trying to achieve, and whether that outcome remains stable
Boundaries MBTs — Conditions about the operational, regulatory, and structural environment within which execution must succeed
Competition MBTs — Conditions about who the real alternatives are, and whether the competitive frame still reflects reality
Value Proposition MBTs — Conditions about whether the organisation’s distinctive advantage is being maintained by the strategy being pursued

When leaders name MBT conditions explicitly, they transform ambition into tested commitment. The strategy either rests on confirmed conditions — or it is a well-written aspiration waiting for reality to intervene.
✎ Reflection
For your most important current strategic objective: write one MBT condition per checkpoint. Which checkpoint was hardest to complete? What does that tell you?

What Gets Overlooked
Boundaries. The CEO holds the vision and drives narrative — but operational friction is rarely in the chief executive’s focus until execution stalls significantly.
⚠ Symptom: “Why are we not seeing the results when our strategy is clear?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Boundaries checkpoint forces explicit naming of the regulatory, structural, and behavioural friction standing between the vision and its delivery. Vision without friction-mapping is only a speech.
✓ Right question: “What specific conditions must remain true for execution to sustain the pace we’ve planned for?”
What Gets Overlooked
Arena. The CFO tracks whether the model works — but whether the underlying customer demand is still real and growing is often outside the financial reporting frame.
⚠ Symptom: “The model works… so why is performance lagging?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Arena checkpoint reframes financial health as dependent on customer-need relevance. Revenue can be temporarily maintained even as the underlying arena is shifting away from your value proposition.
✓ Right question: “Is the customer end-game we designed this model around still the right end-game?”
What Gets Overlooked
Competition. Operational leaders optimise the machine — but if the machine is serving the wrong arena, efficiency just accelerates the organisation in the wrong direction.
⚠ Symptom: “We’ve optimised everything — what are we missing?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Competition checkpoint asks: who else is solving the customer’s problem, even those who look nothing like us? Operational excellence means nothing if the alternatives are more convenient for the customer.
✓ Right question: “Are our efficiency gains making us meaningfully more competitive against the real alternatives customers have?”
What Gets Overlooked
Competition. People alignment and engagement are the CHRO’s primary focus — but a highly engaged team executing the wrong strategy still loses to a competitor solving the problem better.
⚠ Symptom: “Our people are committed — why isn’t it translating?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Competition checkpoint reveals that motivation and alignment are necessary but insufficient if strategic direction points at the wrong competitive target. Energy without direction is enthusiasm without results.
✓ Right question: “Are we aligning our people’s energy toward the right competitive arena, or building capability for yesterday’s contest?”
What Gets Overlooked
Arena. Technical delivery is the CTO’s primary accountability — but whether the solution addresses the customer’s actual end-game (functional, emotional, social) is often assumed and left untested.
⚠ Symptom: “We delivered the system — why isn’t adoption there?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals
The Arena checkpoint asks: did we build for what the customer is actually trying to achieve — or for the specification handed to us? Adoption requires arena-alignment as well as technical delivery.
✓ Right question: “Does this solution address the functional, emotional, and social outcome the customer is actually pursuing?”
What Gets Overlooked
Boundaries. The CMO creates demand — but if the operational infrastructure cannot fulfil that demand, the campaign creates frustration and brand damage.
⚠ Symptom: “We created demand — why can’t we fulfil it?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals
The Boundaries checkpoint identifies the internal and external friction that must remain within tolerance for demand to convert to delivered value. Demand without delivery capacity is brand erosion.
✓ Right question: “Do our operational boundaries allow us to fulfil the demand our marketing is designed to generate?”
What Gets Overlooked
Value Proposition. Revenue growth is the CCO’s scorecard — but growing by winning the wrong business can dilute the organisation’s distinctive identity and long-term positioning.
⚠ Symptom: “We’re closing deals — but at what cost to who we are?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals
The Value Proposition checkpoint asks: does this contract strengthen or dilute our distinctive edge? Not all revenue is strategic revenue. Some growth makes the organisation less coherent.
✓ Right question: “Does this deal sharpen our value architecture or compromise it for short-term volume?”
What Gets Overlooked
Arena. Cost reduction and supply chain resilience are the CPO’s primary mandate — but savings that are not connected to the customer’s end-game do not translate into strategic progress.
⚠ Symptom: “We’ve saved money — but has it actually mattered?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Arena checkpoint asks: does this procurement decision improve our ability to deliver on the customer’s actual need? Cost efficiency that doesn’t serve the customer’s end-game is operational tidiness.
✓ Right question: “Does this cost initiative strengthen our ability to compete in the arena our customers actually operate in?”
What Gets Overlooked
Boundaries. Strategy clarity is the CSO’s domain — but without explicit identification of operational friction, strategies that are coherent in design break down repeatedly in execution.
⚠ Symptom: “Why does execution keep breaking after alignment?”
What the ABCV Checkpoint Reveals

The Boundaries checkpoint identifies structural, cultural, and regulatory friction points that strategy must be designed around. Clarity without friction-mapping is strategy without implementation physics.
✓ Right question: “Which operational friction points have we built our strategy around — and which are we still hoping won’t materialise?”
✎ Reflection
Having explored your role’s typical blind spot: what is one MBT condition in that checkpoint that your organisation is currently assuming without confirmation? What would it take to verify it?

content: Each scenario below describes a real-world strategy that failed. Your task: identify the investigation question that would have exposed the failure, and the ABCV checkpoint it belongs to. Choose carefully — wrong answers detonate.

💣 Mine 1 — The Ghost Ship

A SaaS platform achieved 85% retention in year one. By year three, churn reached 70%. Nothing in the product changed. Support tickets were low. The platform worked exactly as designed. Post-exit interviews revealed: customers had changed what they were trying to achieve — and the platform never followed.
SELECT THE INVESTIGATION QUESTION
SELECT THE ABCV CHECKPOINT
💣 Mine 2 — The Ferrari in the Mud

A leading logistics firm invested R120m in a new digital operations platform. Eighteen months in, less than 30% of staff were using it consistently. Field teams had developed workarounds. Middle management had quietly reverted to spreadsheets. The system was technically excellent. The organisation was not designed to absorb it.
SELECT THE INVESTIGATION QUESTION
SELECT THE ABCV CHECKPOINT
💣 Mine 3 — The Invisible Disruption

A financial advisory firm was ranked #1 in client satisfaction for four consecutive years. Then revenue began declining. No competitor had taken their clients. No scandal. No service failure. The problem: a fintech app was letting clients self-manage what the firm had always managed for them — and clients preferred it for 60% of use cases.
SELECT THE INVESTIGATION QUESTION
SELECT THE ABCV CHECKPOINT
💣 Mine 4 — The Identity Crisis

A boutique consulting firm built its reputation on deep-sector expertise and bespoke strategy work. Under revenue pressure, they began accepting large implementation contracts — work that paid well but required different skills, different team profiles, and a different culture. Within two years, they won more work but lost their most experienced strategists and their distinctiveness with clients who valued exactly what they had been.

top: ABCV-MBT — The Four Checkpoints of Strategic Integrity

Well-written OKRs can still fail. They fail when the strategic conditions they assumed were never verified. ABCV-MBT gives you four precision checkpoints that separate strategies that hold from strategies that break.
